name: Post-finasteride syndrome concerns

lead: Post-finasteride syndrome is a proposed condition of sexual, mood and cognitive symptoms reported to continue after stopping finasteride. It is not a recognised diagnosis, and incidence and causation are debated.
Regulators have added warnings: the FDA in 2012 on persistent sexual effects and the EMA in 2025 on suicidal thoughts.

paras: Proposed explanations include lowered neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone, epigenetic changes and androgen-receptor changes. None is established in humans.
Reported effects include erectile dysfunction, low libido, depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation. No approved treatment exists, and evidence is limited to surveys and retrospective studies.

lead: Post-finasteride syndrome (PFS) is a proposed condition in which sexual, psychological and physical symptoms are reported to persist after stopping finasteride, a prescription 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor used for male pattern hair loss and prostate enlargement. It is not recognised as a formal diagnosis in ICD or DSM, and its validity and incidence are debated.[1]

Reported symptoms include low libido, erectile dysfunction, depression, anxiety, cognitive complaints and fatigue.[2][1] The FDA updated finasteride labelling in 2012 to describe persistent sexual side effects, and the European Medicines Agency confirmed in 2025 that suicidal thoughts can occur.[2] A 2019 BMJ editorial called the syndrome ill-defined and controversial, while other researchers consider it real.[2]
In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, PFS concerns are a central debate shaping decisions on whether to use finasteride.

paras: Symptoms reported as persisting after discontinuation include sexual (low libido, erectile dysfunction, orgasm and ejaculate changes), psychological (depression, anxiety, panic, suicidal ideation), cognitive (brain fog) and physical complaints (fatigue, muscle weakness, dry skin, gynecomastia).[2][1] Dutasteride has been linked to similar persistent sexual effects.[1]

Incidence is uncertain because of variable reporting and no agreed diagnostic criteria.[2] A 2017 review of about 12,000 patients found persistent erectile dysfunction of at least 90 days in 1.4 percent, falling to 0.8 percent in men aged 16 to 42.[2] A 2019 systematic review found three studies showing full reversibility and eleven describing irreversible events.[2]

A 2011 survey of 71 men by Irwig and Kolukula reported persistent sexual symptoms lasting an average of 40 months after stopping, and a 2012 follow-up reported higher depression scores in former users than controls; lower allopregnanolone in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma was reported in 2013 and 2017 studies.[1] A 2021 meta-analysis found associations with depression, suicidal ideation and sexual dysfunction after discontinuation, with limited evidence quality.[2]
Critics attribute reports to nocebo effects, pre-existing conditions or selection bias from online support groups, and note that some research is funded by patient advocacy groups.[1]

Finasteride lowers DHT and neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone, which modulates GABA-A receptors.[2] Other hypotheses include epigenetic changes in SRD5A2 and androgen-receptor changes; these remain unproven in humans, and no known biological mechanism is established.[2][1]

The FDA updated labelling in 2012; the EMA began a review in October 2024 and in 2025 confirmed suicidal thoughts as a side effect, mostly with the 1 mg dose.[2] Merck faced about 1,370 product liability lawsuits by 2016; most settled for a lump sum of US$4.3 million by 2018.[2] The Post-Finasteride Syndrome Foundation was established in 2012.[1]

No approved treatments exist. Options discussed include hormone-modifying agents, cognitive behavioural therapy and investigational topical pirenzepine under an expanded access programme, but evidence is limited.[1]

Studies are mostly surveys, retrospective reviews and pharmacovigilance analyses; no randomized trials establishing PFS were found. Findings include the Irwig surveys, a 2017 review of about 12,000 patients, a 2019 systematic review and a 2021 meta-analysis, all with limitations.[2][1]

lore.intro: Forum discussion of PFS spans personal accounts, alternative mechanisms and scepticism about its existence.[3]
